Fact.Name: Eligible children for the adoption credit (Form 8839 Part II columns)
Fact.Description:
One item per eligible CHILD for whom the taxpayer claims the adoption credit — NOT one item per adoption attempt — the printed "Child 1 / Child 2 / Child 3" columns of Form 8839 Part II. Per-child lines 2-6, 10, 11a and 11b live on the item; line 11c sums the per-child line 11b amounts and line 12 sums the per-child line 11a amounts. Faithful input: one item per child, never a pre-summed scalar; all summing is the engine's job. The collection is UNBOUNDED — the printed three-column limit is a presentation constraint (i8839 line 13 directs a continuation statement for more than three children), not an arithmetic one. Absent on a return with no adoption, which is what keeps the gated aggregates at $0.
SCREEN GUIDANCE — MULTIPLE ATTEMPTS AT ONE CHILD COMBINE ONTO ONE ITEM. i8839 "Attempted Adoptions of U.S. Children": "the dollar limitation requires you to combine the qualified adoption expenses you paid if you made more than one attempt to adopt one eligible U.S. child. When you combine the amounts you spent, complete only the 'Child 1' line. Don't report the additional attempt(s) on the 'Child 2' or 'Child 3' line." The add-item flow must ask, before creating a NEW item, whether this is a further attempt to adopt a child already entered — an unsuccessful attempt on one child plus a later successful adoption of a DIFFERENT child is still ONE item, the successfully-adopted child's (i8839 Example 1). Each item's ../writableQualifiedExpenses is the SUM of every attempt's expenses toward that one child, not the latest attempt alone.
THE ANSWER HAS NOWHERE TO LAND YET, and that is named rather than implied. The graph cannot detect a mis-split intake — two items for one child compute exactly as two truly separate eligible children — so this rule is today a screen instruction with no field recording the answer, invisible to the graph and to a later reviewer. The field it needs is a per-item Boolean /form8839Children/*/writableChildCombinesEarlierAttempt ("Is this a further attempt to adopt a child you have already entered?"), asked before a NEW item is created, with its own the application routing row. It is OWED, not built here.

Fact.Name: Eligible child label (stable identity)
Fact.Description: A human-referenceable label for this eligible child (Form 8839 Part I "Child's name"). Plays no part in any computation; a faithful-record field carrying the stable identity so incremental intake is idempotent (re-running yields the same items; adding or replacing one child's document touches exactly that item). OPTIONAL (three-state): unanswered leaves the child unlabeled and changes no tax value.

Fact.Name: Qualified adoption expenses for this child (Form 8839 line 5)
Fact.Description: The qualified adoption expenses the taxpayer paid for THIS eligible child, entered in this child's column on Form 8839 line 5 — reasonable and necessary expenses directly related to the legal adoption (adoption/attorney fees, court costs, travel). Must EXCLUDE any expenses reimbursed by an employer under a written qualified adoption assistance program (Part III, not modelled here) and any amounts funded by a government program. Integer cents; Min 0. OPTIONAL (three-state): unanswered means no qualified expenses for this child and is resolved to 0 by ../qualifiedExpenses (a special-needs child may legitimately have none). WHEN THIS CHILD REPRESENTS MORE THAN ONE ADOPTION ATTEMPT (see /form8839Children's combining rule): this is the COMBINED total of every attempt's expenses toward this one child, e.g. a $9,000 failed attempt plus $12,000 on a later successful adoption of the same child enters $21,000 here, not two items of $9,000 and $12,000 (i8839 Example 3).

Fact.Name: Of the expenses entered for this child, the amount the employer reimbursed (i8839 Line 5 CAUTION)
Fact.Description:
How much of the amount entered in ../writableQualifiedExpenses for THIS child was reimbursed by the taxpayer's employer under a written qualified adoption assistance program. The printed instruction is a CAUTION on Line 5, not a form line: "Expenses reimbursed by your employer under a written qualified adoption assistance program aren't qualified adoption expenses and must not be entered on line 5." A taxpayer who follows that instruction has already netted, and the correct answer here is $0; a taxpayer who entered what they PAID answers the reimbursement, and ../line5 nets it out. Either way the printed line 5 comes out right, which is why the question is phrased against the entry rather than against the adoption.
WHY THIS INTAKE EXISTS. Without it nothing computed or checked the reduction, so the SAME dollars could take the section 137 exclusion in Part III and the section 23 credit in Part II. i8839 Purpose of Form states the interaction and the ordering in one paragraph: "you can't claim both a credit and exclusion for the same expenses" and "For purposes of calculating the adoption credit in Part II, Qualified Adoption Expenses don't include expenses reimbursed by an employer under a written qualified adoption assistance program ... For this reason, you must complete Form 8839, Part III, before you can figure the credit, if any, in Part II. But see Child with special needs." The published Example 1 is the arithmetic: $10,000 of qualified adoption expenses, $4,000 reimbursed by the employer, "your maximum adoption credit is limited to $6,000 ($10,000 - $4,000)". Direction taxpayer-FAVOURABLE, so no complaint surfaces it.
WHY IT IS PER CHILD. The credit's expense base is per child (the Part II columns), and so is the exclusion's line 22. The W-2 box 12 code T total is per W-2 and never per child (the B1 landing's measured cross-check), so only a per-child intake can make the subtraction computable at all.
INTEGER CENTS; Min 0. OPTIONAL (three-state), and the unanswered state is NOT simply "no reduction": ../employerReimbursedExpenses defaults it to $0, and ../hasUnattestedEmployerReimbursement refuses the one state in which that default would hand out the double benefit — a child carrying BOTH a positive line 22 and positive entered expenses with this question unanswered. See that fact for why a presumption was rejected in favour of a refusal.

Fact.Name: Prior-year Form 8839 amount for this child (Form 8839 line 3)
Fact.Description: If a Form 8839 was filed for a prior year for THIS same child, the total of the amounts shown on lines 3 and 6 (or corresponding line) of the last Form 8839 filed for the child — entered in this child's column on line 3. Reduces this child's $17,280 maximum (line 4 = line 2 - line 3). Integer cents; Min 0. OPTIONAL (three-state): unanswered is the "No. Enter -0-" branch, resolved to 0 by ../priorYearExpenses.

Fact.Name: This child has special needs (i8839 "Child with special needs")
Fact.Description: True if THIS eligible child is a U.S. child with special needs whose adoption became final in 2025 (a state or Indian tribal government determined the child can't/shouldn't be returned home and won't be adopted without assistance). When true, this child's credit is the FULL $17,280 (minus any prior-year amount) REGARDLESS of the actual qualified expenses — even if the taxpayer paid no qualified expenses for the child. OPTIONAL (three-state): unanswered is resolved to false by ../hasSpecialNeeds (not special needs).

Fact.Name: Divided $17,280 limit: a non-spouse also paid qualified expenses for this child (Form 8839 line 2)
Fact.Description: True if the taxpayer AND another person who is NOT the taxpayer's spouse (if filing jointly) EACH paid qualified adoption expenses to adopt THIS same eligible child, so the $17,280 per-child limit on line 2 "must be divided between the two of you" by agreement (i8839 Line 2). When true, the taxpayer's agreed share is entered in ../writableDividedLimitShare and becomes this child's line 2 (capped at the full $17,280); when false or unanswered the child takes the full $17,280 line-2 maximum. OPTIONAL (three-state): unanswered is resolved to false by ../sharesLimitWithNonSpouse (no non-spouse co-adopter => the full limit), so this changes no value on any return that does not assert a shared adoption. This is the writable that makes a divided-limit adoption REPRESENTABLE so the engine no longer silently gives a non-spouse co-adopter the full $17,280.

Fact.Name: Your agreed share of the $17,280 limit for this child (Form 8839 line 2)
Fact.Description: The taxpayer's agreed share of the $17,280 per-child limit when a non-spouse also paid qualified expenses for THIS same child (../writableSharesLimitWithNonSpouse true): "You can divide it in any way you both agree. Enter your share of the $17,280 limit on line 2 for that child" (i8839 Line 2). Integer cents; Min 0. Only consulted when the shared-limit flag is true; a share above $17,280 is capped at the full per-child maximum by ../line2. OPTIONAL (three-state): unanswered is resolved to $0 by ../dividedLimitShare — so a return that asserts a shared adoption but omits the share takes the conservative $0 line-2 branch (no credit) rather than silently claiming the full limit (World-#1-safe).

Fact.Name: Qualified adoption expenses for this child, complete-safe (Form 8839 line 5)
Fact.Description: = ../writableQualifiedExpenses when answered, else $0 (the IsComplete pattern). Required so an unanswered per-child expense cannot make the line-11c/line-12 CollectionSum Incomplete.

Fact.Name: Employer-reimbursed part of this child's entered expenses, complete-safe (i8839 Line 5 CAUTION)
Fact.Description: = ../writableEmployerReimbursedExpenses when answered, else $0 (the IsComplete pattern every other per-child money leaf on this form uses). The $0 tail is the RIGHT default for the population that carries no employer-provided adoption benefit for this child at all — there is nothing to have reimbursed — and it is the right default for a filer who followed the printed Line 5 CAUTION and entered a net figure. It is NOT a safe default for a child that carries a positive line 22 AND positive entered expenses; that state is refused by ../hasUnattestedEmployerReimbursement rather than defaulted, so silence can never buy the double benefit.

Fact.Name: Qualified adoption expenses for this child, net of employer reimbursement (Form 8839 line 5)
Fact.Description:
Form 8839 line 5, this child's column, as the printed form defines it: the qualified adoption expenses paid for this child MINUS the part of them the employer reimbursed under a written qualified adoption assistance program, floored at $0. The floor is structural — a reimbursement larger than the entered expenses leaves no qualified expenses, never a negative expense base.
THIS IS THE FACT THAT ENDS THE DOUBLE BENEFIT. Without it, ../line6 would read ../qualifiedExpenses directly, so the same dollars could appear on line 5 as the credit's expense base and on line 22 as the exclusion's employer benefit, and the taxpayer received both. The printed rule is not a computation the form performs — it is the Line 5 CAUTION telling the filer what not to enter — so the dictionary makes it computable by asking the two things the taxpayer actually knows (what was entered, how much of it was reimbursed) and deriving the printed line. That is the faithful-input posture the rest of this collection already takes.
ONLY THE NON-SPECIAL-NEEDS ARM READS IT, and that is the printed rule rather than an oversight. i8839's own sentence ends "But see Child with special needs", and the special-needs instruction says to enter $17,280 minus the prior-year amount on line 5 "even if ... you didn't have any qualified adoption expenses for this child" — so a special-needs child's line 5 is a statutory figure, not a receipt total, and ../line6 keeps taking ../line4 directly for that child.
BYTE-IDENTICAL ON THE COMMITTED CORPUS: ../writableEmployerReimbursedExpenses is a new intake, absent on all 18 scenarios that declare /form8839Children, so ../employerReimbursedExpenses is $0 and this fact equals ../qualifiedExpenses everywhere today.

Fact.Name: Prior-year Form 8839 amount for this child, complete-safe (Form 8839 line 3)
Fact.Description: = ../writablePriorYearExpenses when answered, else $0 (the "No. Enter -0-" default).

Fact.Name: This child has special needs, complete-safe
Fact.Description: = ../writableHasSpecialNeeds when answered, else false.

Fact.Name: Divided-limit flag for this child, complete-safe (Form 8839 line 2)
Fact.Description: = ../writableSharesLimitWithNonSpouse when answered, else false (no non-spouse co-adopter => the full $17,280 line-2 limit applies). Complete-safe so an unanswered flag cannot make ../line2 (and the per-child credit chain) Incomplete.

Fact.Name: Your agreed share of the $17,280 limit, complete-safe (Form 8839 line 2)
Fact.Description: = ../writableDividedLimitShare when answered, else $0 (the conservative default when a divided-limit adoption is asserted but no share is entered — a $0 line-2 branch, never the full $17,280). Only consulted by ../line2 when ../sharesLimitWithNonSpouse is true.

Fact.Name: This child was under age 18 when the expenses were paid, by year of birth and the paid-before-18 answer, complete-safe (Form 8839 Part I column (b))
Fact.Description:
True when ../writableChildYearOfBirth is answered and shows a birth year of 2007 or later. A child born in 2007 turned 18 during 2025 and is an eligible child for the part of the year they were under age 18, which is exactly what the printed definition allows ("Any child under age 18. If the child turned 18 during the year, the child is an eligible child for the part of the year they were under age 18"); a child born in 2006 or earlier was 19 or older for the whole of 2025 and can reach the eligible-child definition only through ../childBornBefore2008AndDisabled. The form asks for the YEAR only, never a date, so the boundary can only be drawn at the birth year, and it is drawn on the side the printed part-year sentence names — 2007 eligible.
A CHILD BORN IN 2006 OR EARLIER CAN STILL BE AN ELIGIBLE CHILD FOR EXPENSES PAID BEFORE AGE 18. Expenses reach the 2025 form from earlier years: a domestic adoption's expenses paid in 2024 are allowed in 2025 (the year after payment), and a foreign adoption's are allowed in the year it becomes final, whenever paid. The part-year sentence makes the child eligible for the part of the year the child was under 18, so expenses paid before the 18th birthday are for an eligible child. A child born in 2006 (18 during 2024; domestic or foreign) or earlier (foreign only) is therefore eligible when ../writableChildExpensesPaidBeforeAge18 is answered Yes. A domestic child born in 2005 or earlier was 18 before 2024, so no expense on the 2025 form was paid before that birthday, and the answer is not read for such a child.
UNANSWERED RESOLVES TRUE, AND THAT IS THE WEAKER OF TWO WRONG ANSWERS, HELD DELIBERATELY. A blank column (b) does not by itself disqualify a child, because losing a credit on silence is the taxpayer-ADVERSE direction and most adopted children are in fact under 18. But neither should the credit be taken silently by a filer who was never asked the question, and the right answer to that is a REFUSAL — a child with a blank column (b), an unchecked column (c) and a computed Part II credit should block submission until the year is entered, in the shape /knockoutUnattestedAdoptionReimbursement already uses. That refusal is specified and OWED, not built: a new submission-blocking fact needs a scope-sidecar row, a regenerated scope ledger, a refusal-successor allowlist row and membership in flow:/flowIsKnockedOut, none of which this module can write. Until it lands, a filer who is never asked column (b) keeps the credit, and that is a known open exposure rather than a considered rule. Combines with ../childBornBefore2008AndDisabled in ../childMeetsEligibleChildDefinition.

Fact.Name: This child was born before 2008 and is disabled, complete-safe (Form 8839 Part I column (c))
Fact.Description: = ../writableChildBornBefore2008AndDisabled when answered, else false. The printed column (c) box is itself the compound condition ("born before 2008 and disabled"); a disabled individual is an eligible child regardless of age at the time of adoption, so this box is the SOLE eligibility path for a child who fails ../childAgeEligible.

Fact.Name: This child meets the section 23(d)(2) eligible-child definition
Fact.Description: True when ../childAgeEligible OR ../childBornBefore2008AndDisabled holds — the two printed paths to being an "eligible child" (i8839 Definitions, "Eligible Child"): under 18, or disabled regardless of age. Gates the Part II credit chain (../line2) and the Part III exclusion chain (../line19), so a plainly ineligible child (an adult, entered year of birth well before 2008, with the column (c) box unchecked) computes neither a credit nor an exclusion. The Part III gate follows IRC 137(d), which gives "qualified adoption expenses" the section 23(d) meaning.

Fact.Name: This child is a foreign child, complete-safe (Form 8839 Part I column (e))
Fact.Description: = ../writableChildIsForeignChild when answered, else false. Unanswered defaults to "not foreign" so a silent column cannot bar a domestic adoption's credit or exclusion; only an affirmed foreign-child box, combined with an unaffirmed finality box, triggers ../childForeignAndNotFinal.

Fact.Name: This child's adoption became final in 2025 or earlier, complete-safe (Form 8839 Part I column (g))
Fact.Description: = ../writableChildAdoptionFinalIn2025OrEarlier when answered, else false. The conservative default: only consulted when ../childIsForeignChild is true, and an unanswered finality box on an affirmed foreign child cannot prove the finality section 23(e)(1) requires before the credit or exclusion is available, so silence reads as "not yet final" rather than granting the benefit on an unproven claim.

Fact.Name: This child is a foreign child whose adoption has not become final (bars the credit and exclusion)
Fact.Description: True when ../childIsForeignChild is true AND ../childAdoptionFinalIn2025OrEarlier is false. i8839: "If the eligible child is a foreign child, you can't take the adoption credit or exclusion unless the adoption becomes final" — an unconditional bar, not a phaseout. Gates BOTH the Part II credit chain (../line2) and the Part III exclusion chain (../line19) — the whole per-child computation, on Not(foreign AND NOT final). A foreign adoption not yet final still routes any employer-provided benefits received to Form 1040 line 1f in full (i8839, "If you received employer-provided adoption benefits ... and the adoption didn't become final ... you must include the benefits in the total entered on line 1f") — that full-inclusion routing is untouched by this fact; this fact only stops the exclusion/credit from ALSO applying.

Fact.Name: Maximum adoption credit for this child, after any divided-limit split (Form 8839 line 2)
Fact.Description:
Form 8839 line 2, this child's column. Normally the full $17,280 per-child maximum (/adoptionMaxCreditPerChild). BUT when the taxpayer and a non-spouse each paid qualified expenses to adopt THIS same child (../sharesLimitWithNonSpouse), the $17,280 limit "must be divided between the two of you ... Enter your share of the $17,280 limit on line 2 for that child" (i8839 Line 2): line 2 becomes the taxpayer's agreed share (../dividedLimitShare), capped at the full $17,280 (a share can never exceed the statutory per-child maximum). This is what stops a non-spouse co-adopter from silently receiving the FULL $17,280 line-2 maximum instead of the agreed share. The rejected alternative was a knockout that denies the credit outright when a divided adoption is asserted; computing the agreed share is more faithful to the taxpayer's actual entitlement and is World-#1-safe (an unanswered share defaults to $0, never the full limit).
ELIGIBILITY GATE: $0 outright when this child fails ../childMeetsEligibleChildDefinition (not under 18 and not the disabled exception) or trips ../childForeignAndNotFinal (a foreign child whose adoption has not become final) — checked FIRST, before the divided-limit split, since an ineligible child's line 2 is $0 regardless of any agreed share. Both gates read cells already collected on Form 8839 Part I; no new intake.

Fact.Name: Maximum credit less prior-year amount, this child (Form 8839 line 4)
Fact.Description: Form 8839 line 4, this child's column = line 2 (the per-child maximum, $17,280 or the taxpayer's divided share) - line 3 (the prior-year Form 8839 amount for this same child), floored at $0 (a credit basis cannot be negative when a small divided share is netted against a larger prior-year amount).

Fact.Name: This child's credit before the MAGI phaseout (Form 8839 line 6)
Fact.Description:
Form 8839 line 6, this child's column = smaller of line 4 or line 5 (this child's qualified expenses). EXCEPTION: for a U.S. child with special needs whose adoption became final in 2025, line 5 is set to line 4 ($17,280 minus the prior-year amount) regardless of actual expenses (i8839 "Special needs adoption"), so line 6 = line 4. Modeled directly: special-needs => line 4 ; otherwise => min(line 4, line 5).
LINE 5. The ordinary arm reads ../line5 — the printed line 5, qualified expenses NET of the employer reimbursement — not ../qualifiedExpenses, the raw entry. That is the printed rule: i8839 Purpose of Form says qualified adoption expenses for Part II "don't include expenses reimbursed by an employer under a written qualified adoption assistance program", and its Example 1 turns $10,000 of expenses with a $4,000 reimbursement into a $6,000 maximum credit. The special-needs arm is deliberately untouched: the same sentence ends "But see Child with special needs", and that child's line 5 is the statutory $17,280 less the prior-year amount regardless of receipts. BYTE-IDENTICAL on every committed scenario, where the new reimbursement intake is absent and ../line5 equals ../qualifiedExpenses.

Fact.Name: This child's expenses and employer benefits contradict each other with no reimbursement answer
Fact.Description:
TRUE for a child that carries BOTH a positive Form 8839 line 22 (employer-provided adoption benefits for this child) AND positive entered qualified expenses, while ../writableEmployerReimbursedExpenses is UNANSWERED. That is the one state in which the graph cannot tell whether the same dollars are being claimed twice, and it is the permanent data-completeness residue of the C4-7 fill.
WHY A REFUSAL AND NOT A DEFAULT, decided here rather than left implicit. Two defaults were available and both are wrong in this state. Defaulting the reduction to $0 grants the double benefit on silence — the taxpayer-FAVOURABLE direction, which is exactly the class this sweep exists to close. Defaulting it to the line-22 amount (or to min(line 22, expenses)) double-subtracts for the compliant filer, because the printed Line 5 CAUTION tells that filer their entry is ALREADY net: "Expenses reimbursed by your employer ... must not be entered on line 5." The two readings differ by the whole reimbursement and nothing on the return discriminates them, so neither may be asserted on the taxpayer's behalf. The honest answer is to ask, and to refuse the return until the question is answered — the refusal shape the C4-7 contract names as (b), kept as the residue of the (a) fill rather than instead of it.
NARROW BY CONSTRUCTION. It cannot fire for a child with no employer benefits (nothing to reimburse), nor for a child with no entered expenses (no credit base to reduce), nor once the question is answered with any amount including $0, nor for a special-needs child (../hasSpecialNeeds). A special-needs child's line 6 takes line 4, the full per-child amount whatever was paid or reimbursed (i8839 Special needs adoption), and line 24 reads line 21 or line 22, never the reimbursement, so no answer to the question can move a dollar for that child. Refusing the return on it would block a filing the source says to compute.
Gated on IsComplete of the WRITABLE, never on a complete-safe wrapper: ../employerReimbursedExpenses is Complete on every return by construction, so testing it would make this fact always false.

Fact.Name: Dollars at risk of the exclusion/credit double benefit for this child
Fact.Description: The dollars this child could take twice while ../hasUnattestedEmployerReimbursement is true: the smaller of the employer-provided benefits (line 22) and the entered qualified expenses, because only the overlap can be claimed on both sides. $0 whenever the contradiction is absent. It exists as a DOLLAR rather than as a second boolean so the return-level refusal can be built with the gated CollectionSum idiom this module already uses five times (/adoptionLine11cRefundable, /adoptionLine12, /adoptionLine23TotalEmployerBenefits, /adoptionLine30ExcludedBenefits, /adoptionTotalPriorYearExpenses) rather than with an unproven boolean aggregation — and it is the number a reviewer wants when asking how much the refusal is protecting.

Fact.Name: Total dollars at risk of the exclusion/credit double benefit, all children
Fact.Description: The sum across /form8839Children of ../unattestedEmployerReimbursementExposure. GATED on IsComplete(/form8839Children) for the reason /adoptionLine11cRefundable states: CollectionSum seeds Result(zero, vect.complete), so a bare sum over the undeclared collection every non-adoption return has would resolve Incomplete and cascade — here into a submission refusal, which is the worst possible place for an Incomplete to land.

Fact.Name: Refusal: employer adoption benefits and adoption expenses for the same child, reimbursement unanswered
Fact.Description:
The return carries at least one eligible child with BOTH a positive Form 8839 line 22 and positive entered qualified expenses, and no answer to how much of those expenses the employer reimbursed. The section 137 exclusion and the section 23 credit would then be figured on dollars that may be the same dollars, which i8839 Purpose of Form forbids in terms ("you can't claim both a credit and exclusion for the same expenses") and IRC 23(d)(1)(D) and 137(d) forbid: an expense reimbursed under an employer program is not a qualified adoption expense for the credit, and the exclusion reaches it without regard to that reimbursement. A special-needs child never trips it (see the per-child predicate). The graph cannot resolve the ambiguity from anything else on the return, so the return is refused until the question is answered — see /form8839Children/*/hasUnattestedEmployerReimbursement for why neither available default is safe.
THIS IS THE PERMANENT RESIDUE, not a placeholder: answering the question with ANY amount, including $0, clears it, so the refusal collapses to nothing the moment the intake is asked. The interview obligation that closes it in practice is an application routing row for /form8839Children/*/writableEmployerReimbursedExpenses, asked whenever a child's line 22 is positive.
COMPLETE-FALSE ON EVERY COMMITTED SCENARIO, and structurally rather than by luck: no committed scenario answers /form8839Children/*/writableEmployerAdoptionBenefits at all, so every child's line 22 is $0 and the leading conjunct of the per-child predicate cannot hold. The aggregation beneath it is gated on IsComplete(/form8839Children), so a return with no adoption resolves this Complete-false without touching the collection.
A MEMBER OF THE KNOCKOUT UNION: flow.xml's /flowIsKnockedOut names this fact in a <Dependency module="form8839" path="/knockoutUnattestedAdoptionReimbursement" />, so a true value here blocks submission of the return. That membership changes nothing else about the guard — its scope-sidecar row, its test_refusal_trigger_allowlist and test_refusal_successor_allowlist rows, and its INTAKE-GROUPS retirement trigger (the Form 8839 reimbursement pair) all stand as written.

Fact.Name: This child's phaseout reduction (Form 8839 line 10)
Fact.Description: Form 8839 line 10, this child's column = line 6 x line 9 = line 6 x (/adoptionPhaseoutFractionThousandths / 1000), rounded to whole dollars. The phaseout FRACTION (line 9) is per return; the form directs "Multiply EACH amount on line 6 by line 9", so the same fraction is applied to every child's line 6 independently. 0 when MAGI <= $259,190 (line 9 = 0).

Fact.Name: This child's credit after phaseout (Form 8839 line 11a)
Fact.Description: Form 8839 line 11a, this child's column = line 6 - line 10 (this child's adoption credit after the MAGI phaseout). Equals line 6 when MAGI <= $259,190; 0 when MAGI >= $299,190. Summed across children by /adoptionLine12.

Fact.Name: This child's refundable credit, capped at $5,000 (Form 8839 line 11b)
Fact.Description: Form 8839 line 11b, this child's column = smaller of this child's line 11a or $5,000. THE $5,000 REFUNDABLE CAP IS PER CHILD, NOT PER RETURN — i8839 states it twice ("The amount of the refundable credit portion is determined separately for each eligible child"; "The refundable credit amount is determined per eligible child. The amounts per child are then added together for a total, refundable credit amount"). Summed across children by /adoptionLine11cRefundable (line 11c), which is Form 8839 line 13 and Form 1040 line 30. A two-child family each at or above the cap therefore receives $10,000 refundable, not $5,000.

Fact.Name: Adoption credit carryforward IN from prior years (Form 8839 line 15)
Fact.Description: Unused nonrefundable adoption credit carried forward INTO 2025 from prior years' returns (Form 8839 line 15, from the Adoption Credit Carryforward Worksheet in the 2024 Form 8839 instructions). Adds to the current-year nonrefundable base (line 16 = line 14 + line 15). Any carryforward is a NONrefundable credit only -- it can never become refundable. Per return, not per child. Integer cents; Min 0. Optional -- absent => complete-safe 0.

Fact.Name: MFS: 2020 carryforward vintage meets its origin-year filing condition
Fact.Description: For this positive carryforward vintage, were you unmarried in the year of origin, or, if married, did you file a joint return for that year? Answer yes only when the origin-year condition is met. Asked only for the corresponding positive vintage on an MFS return; an unanswered required answer leaves this vintage unavailable rather than silently allowing or denying it.

Fact.Name: Adoption MFS: eligible child lived in the taxpayer's home more than half of 2025
Fact.Description:
MFS "considered unmarried" test (i8839 "Married Persons Not Filing Jointly"): the eligible child lived in the taxpayer's home for more than half of 2025. Optional — absent => treated as false (not considered unmarried => MFS stays $0, World-#1-safe).
Consumed by /adoptionCreditIsActive, which is what lets an MFS filer reach the credit at all through the "considered unmarried" test. Nothing in this graph computes where an eligible child lived during 2025 — the residency facts the dictionary carries are the dependent tests, which an eligible child under section 23 need not satisfy — so the attestation is the only source. Fact.Name: Filing status permits the adoption credit AND the section 137 exclusion
Fact.Description:
The i8839 "Who Can Take the Adoption Credit or Exclude Employer-Provided Adoption Benefits?" statement (1) test, held as ONE fact for BOTH halves of Form 8839: "Your filing status is single, head of household, qualifying surviving spouse, or married filing jointly. Generally, if you are married, you must file a joint return to take the credit or exclusion. However, if you are married and aren't filing jointly, you may be able to take the credit or exclusion on your own return if you are considered unmarried". One predicate for both halves of Form 8839: the printed heading governs the EXCLUSION as well as the credit, so Part II and Part III both read this one fact.
THE DEFECT IT ENDS, measured before the gate existed. An MFS filer who is NOT considered unmarried, with employer-provided adoption benefits entered in Part III, took the full section 137 exclusion: line 30 excluded the benefits and line 31 came out $0, so Form 1040 line 1f carried nothing and AGI omitted money the statute leaves in gross income. Direction: taxpayer-FAVOURABLE, so no complaint surfaces it. Measured witness, run before the gate was added: the barred-MFS fixture resolved /adoptionLine30ExcludedBenefits 4,000, /adoptionLine31TaxableBenefits 0 and /agi 84,325, where the printed rules give 0, 4,000 and 88,325. Pinned by tests/nodes/ty2025/form8839/f8839-part3-mfs-barred-benefits-fully-taxable.

Line 31 is the subtraction and must not be gated directly, or the Yes-branch negative would be reachable for a filer entitled to no exclusion at all. Zeroing line 30 is the printed effect of "you may be able to take the credit or exclusion" failing, and it produces the right line 31 by the form's own arithmetic.

An MFS filer with any attestation unanswered is Complete-FALSE rather than Incomplete, because each attestation is IsComplete-guarded before it is read, so an ineligible filer never over-claims. On a return that answers NO filing status at all, filingStatus:/isFilingStatusMFS is not Complete and this fact is Placeholder, so every consuming When guards with All(IsComplete(this), ...): line 30's leading case does, and /adoptionCreditIsActive reads this fact behind the same All(IsComplete(x), x) wrapper.

Fact.Name: MFS prior-year adoption credit carryforward origin-year exception
Fact.Description:
True for a filer who is married filing separately, has NOT declared any /form8839Children this year, and HAS answered the prior-year carryforward question (/writableAdoptionCreditCarryforwardFromPriorTaxYear). i8839 "Married Persons Not Filing Jointly" closes with a rule distinct from the considered-unmarried test that governs the rest of that section: "a person who is filing separately may claim an adoption credit carryforward from a prior year or years" — the carryforward attaches to the ORIGIN year (consistent with IRC 23(c)(1)/23(f)(1) biting when the expenses first became allowable), not to the filing status of the year the carryforward is used.
THE CARVEOUT IS ALL-OR-NOTHING, AND ONE POPULATION LOSES BY IT. It requires that NO /form8839Children be declared, so a plain-MFS filer who has BOTH new Part II children this year AND a prior-year carryforward does not get it: /adoptionCreditIsActive stays false for that filer, and because Form 8839 line 16 adds /adoptionCarryforwardIn inside that same gate, the CARRYFORWARD is refused along with the current-year credit. Nothing in the printed rule conditions the carryforward on whether the filer has current-year children — it conditions it only on the origin-year return — so that refusal is the taxpayer-ADVERSE direction and is a named residual, not a considered denial. The fix shape, when the project owner wants it: sever /adoptionCarryforwardIn from /adoptionCreditIsActive's eligibility gate so the carryforward leg is available to any MFS filer, leaving the current-year expense leg governed by /adoptionFilingStatusEligible's considered-unmarried test.
THE ORIGIN-YEAR JOINT-RETURN CONDITION IS NOT VERIFIED. The printed rule is conditional: "provided that, if the person was married in the year in which the qualified adoption expenses first became allowable for the credit, the person filed a joint return for that year." This single-year graph has no origin-year filing-status attestation to test that condition (the same limitation /adoptionFilingStatusEligible's own MFS-carryforward note names). Admitting the carryforward without it is the deliberate, disclosed choice here: refusing a usable carryforward is the taxpayer-ADVERSE direction on an already-computed prior-year amount, not the safe one, so silence on the origin-year condition resolves in the filer's favor rather than barring the carryforward outright.
COMPLETE-SAFE: every conjunct is IsComplete-guarded or already complete by construction (Not(IsComplete(...)) is always Complete), so an unanswered filing status or an unanswered carryforward question resolves this fact Complete-false rather than Incomplete or Placeholder — the same canonical shape /adoptionCreditIsActive's own filing-status operand uses.

Fact.Name: Return has Form 8839 adoption-credit inputs AND is eligible (not barred MFS)
Fact.Description:
True when the return has Form 8839 Part II input — at least one /form8839Children item, or a prior-year carryforward — AND the filing status is not a barred married-filing-separately. Gates /refundableAdoptionCredit and /nonrefundableAdoptionCredit so a return with no adoption — OR a barred MFS return — takes the else-0 branch WITHOUT evaluating the tax-liability chain, keeping Form 1040 line 30 and Schedule 3 line 6c byte-identical on scenarios whose credit facts are Placeholder or Incomplete (the branch-gate lesson). The three per-child writables live inside /form8839Children, so the input test is IsComplete(/form8839Children) — always Complete (IsComplete returns complete=true for any operand), false when the collection is undeclared. MFS ELIGIBILITY: married filers generally must file jointly to take the adoption credit (IRC §23; i8839 "Who Can Take the Adoption Credit" / "Married Persons Not Filing Jointly"); MFS is barred EXCEPT for a filer who is considered unmarried (lived apart the last 6 months of 2025 and meets the home/child tests). The gate is Not(MFS) OR (the inlined considered-unmarried test), so a considered-unmarried MFS filer is freed while a plain MFS filer still takes the $0 branch. Still World-#1-safe: an ineligible MFS filer never over-claims (unanswered attestations => false).
MFS CARRYFORWARD-ONLY EXCEPTION: a plain-MFS filer who does NOT meet the considered-unmarried test may still claim a PRIOR-YEAR carryforward with no new Part II children this year (/adoptionMfsCarryforwardOnlyCarveout) — i8839 "Married Persons Not Filing Jointly" closes with a rule distinct from considered-unmarried: the carryforward attaches to the year the expenses first became allowable, not to this year's filing status. Only a PURE carryforward-only return takes this second path: a plain-MFS filer who has new children this year AND a carryforward fails the considered-unmarried test and fails the carveout too, so this gate is false and BOTH legs are refused — including line 16's /adoptionCarryforwardIn, which sits inside this gate. That refusal is a named residual, not a printed rule; see /adoptionMfsCarryforwardOnlyCarveout for the population and the fix shape.
FILING-STATUS OPERAND, COMPLETE-SAFE: /adoptionFilingStatusEligible is read behind the canonical All(IsComplete(x), x) wrapper rather than as a bare All operand. A return that declares /form8839Children with no filing status answered therefore resolves this gate Complete-FALSE rather than Placeholder — no filing status answered means no credit claimed, which is the branch-gate's own posture — and /refundableAdoptionCredit and /nonrefundableAdoptionCredit take their else-0 branch there instead of inheriting a Placeholder. Every return that answers a filing status is unaffected: the eligibility fact is Complete on all of them and the guard operand is then true.

Fact.Name: Form 8839 must be attached to this return (the printed-form render population)
Fact.Description:
The population whose return must carry a printed Form 8839, and the fact the IRS8839 document gate is meant to read. TRUE when EITHER (a) the return actually claims the adoption credit or the section 137 exclusion (/adoptionCreditIsActive — Part II input and an eligible filing status), OR (b) Form 8839 line 31 is not zero, which is exactly the state in which Form 1040 line 1f prints a dollar amount whose printed label is "Employer-provided adoption benefits from Form 8839, line 31".
WHY THIS FACT EXISTS. /adoptionCreditIsActive alone, as a document gate, is FALSE for a married-filing-separately filer who is not considered unmarried, and that filer's benefits are fully taxable — line 30 is zeroed, so line 31 equals line 23 — and line 31 is Form 1040 line 1f. The result would be a 1040 printing a positive line 1f sourced "from Form 8839, line 31" with no Form 8839 anywhere in the return. Disjunct (b) is that population and nothing else.
THE AUTHORITY, stated exactly as far as it goes. There is NO freestanding must-file sentence in the 2025 Instructions for Form 8839 — the instruction never says "you must file Form 8839 if ...", and one is not invented here. What IS printed is (i) the Form 1040 line 1f label, which names Form 8839 line 31 as the source of the amount, so a return reporting that amount must carry the form the amount is figured on, and (ii) i8839 Purpose of Form, "Use Form 8839 to figure your adoption credit and any employer-provided adoption benefits you can exclude from your income" — the exclusion is figured ON this form, so the form is the return's record of the figure. Both halves of disjunct (a) come from the same sentence.
WHY NOT IsComplete(/form8839Children), the alternative the contract named. It is wrong in BOTH directions. It UNDER-includes: a carryforward-only return (line 15 answered, no children collection) has /adoptionCreditIsActive TRUE and prints Schedule 3 line 6c "from Form 8839, line 18" — the identical print contradiction one form over, so keying the gate on the collection would create the defect it was meant to cure. It OVER-includes: it prints the form for every return that merely declares the collection, including the four committed barred/failed-MFS scenarios whose Form 8839 is entirely zeros and whose 1040 says nothing about Form 8839 at all.
BYTE-IDENTICAL ON THE COMMITTED CORPUS, and this is a measurement rather than an argument: no committed scenario carries any employer-provided adoption benefit (/form8839Children/*/writableEmployerAdoptionBenefits is absent on all 18 scenarios that declare the collection), so line 23 = line 30 = line 31 = $0 everywhere and disjunct (b) is false on every one of them. This fact therefore equals /adoptionCreditIsActive on the whole corpus, and the document gate's population does not move until a return reports benefits.
COMPLETE-SAFE, deliberately, in both disjuncts. /adoptionCreditIsActive reads /adoptionFilingStatusEligible as a bare All operand and is therefore Placeholder on a return that declares /form8839Children and answers NO filing status (see /adoptionFilingStatusEligible). A render gate must never be Placeholder (an undetermined gate is an undetermined document), so each disjunct is wrapped in the repo's canonical All(IsComplete(x), x) form and an unanswered upstream contributes Complete-false instead of Placeholder.
EXPORTED: the printed-document gate (dictionary/pdf/2025/gates.tsv and the IRS8839 configuration.yml) is a downstream consumer, so the Export below is the honest wiring.

Fact.Name: Form 8839 line 9 in thousandths, as the division and rounding nodes first produce it
Fact.Description: Line 8 (modified adjusted gross income over the threshold) divided by $40, which is 1000 times line 8 over $40,000, rounded to a whole number of thousandths and capped at 1000, when line 7 is above the threshold; $0 otherwise. This is an intermediate figure and not the printed line. A Dollar division is reduced to cents (half to even) before the outer Round takes it to whole thousandths (half up), so a true quotient a fraction of a cent below one half of a thousandth is rounded up; the cent reduction moves a value by at most half a cent, so the only possible error here is one thousandth too high. /adoptionPhaseoutFractionThousandths corrects that step with exact cent arithmetic.

Fact.Name: 2020 adoption credit carryforward, the expiring lot (Nonrefundable Adoption Credit Carryforward Worksheet—Line 18, line 2)
Fact.Description:

Enter the amount from line 12 of the Adoption Credit Carryforward Worksheet—Line 16 in your 2024 Form 8839 instructions." The rejected alternative was a $0 default, which prints a 2026 carryforward too large by exactly the expiring lot — a favourable silence on a number the filer would rely on next year.
VALIDATION: Dollar, integer cents, Min $0. It is a PART of Form 8839 line 15 and may not exceed it; a larger answer is an input contradiction and /knockoutAdoptionCarryforward2020VintageExceedsLine15 blocks submission until one of the two is corrected.

Fact.Name: Total nonrefundable adoption credit carryforward to 2026 (Nonrefundable Adoption Credit Carryforward Worksheet—Line 18, line 23; REPORTED)
Fact.Description:
The total unused nonrefundable adoption credit the filer carries from 2025 into 2026 — worksheet line 23, the figure Form 8839 line 18's instruction sends the filer to the worksheet for. REPORTED, never applied: this graph files one tax year, so the amount is printed for the filer to carry onto their 2026 Form 8839 line 15, nothing here consumes it, and no 2026 return is filed from it.
WHY ONE PRIOR-YEAR QUESTION MAKES THE TOTAL EXACT. The worksheet spends Form 8839 line 18 against the prior-year lots oldest first (lines 10-18) and the current-year amount last (line 20), so line 19 is the prior lots' residue and line 20 the current year's. Their sum, line 21, is worksheet line 9 — Form 8839 line 16 minus line 18 — however the spending happened to split, because the amount taken from the prior lots and the amount taken from the current year add back to line 18. Line 23 then subtracts line 22, which is line 10: the part of the 2020 lot line 18 did not reach. That is the only lot the five-year window kills, so the total is (line 16 − line 18) − the greater of ($0, the 2020 lot − line 18), which is the SMALLER of (line 16 − line 18) and (line 16 − the 2020 lot) and is how the body below is written, with worksheet line 7 (line 1, Form 8839 line 14, plus the prior lots on lines 2-6) standing where the sentence says line 16; the 2020 vintage is the only year that has to be asked. The five PER-VINTAGE rows the filer transcribes onto next year's worksheet lines 2-6 ship as their own facts over four further vintage questions, and this total deliberately does NOT read them: an Add of the rows would resolve Incomplete whenever any of those four is blank, which would regress an exact figure to a blank box for nothing.
NO PRIOR-YEAR CARRYFORWARD (Form 8839 line 15 = $0, so the worksheet's lines 2-6 are all blank): the worksheet's own No branch — "Enter the amount on line 9 on lines 20 and 23 below; skip all the other lines" — so line 23 = line 16 − line 18. Never negative on either branch, because line 18 is the smaller of line 16 and line 17 on both arms of /nonrefundableAdoptionCredit, which is the fact read here (never the plain arm alone).
UNANSWERED 2020 VINTAGE ON A LINE-15-POSITIVE RETURN: the 2020 writable is read BARE, so this fact resolves INCOMPLETE and the box prints blank. The blank IS the refusal, and it costs the return nothing because nothing consumes this value. There is no "$0 when line 15 is positive" branch anywhere in this body: that would print a carryforward too large by the expiring lot and forfeit nothing visible to the filer until 2026.
A SEPARATE RETURN CARRIES EVERY LOT IT CANNOT USE. On a married-filing-separately return, Form 8839 line 15 holds only the prior lots whose origin year allows them this year, so line 16 can be short of worksheet lines 1-6. The worksheet has no separate-return branch: lines 2-6 take every lot from the 2024 worksheet. Worksheet line 7 is therefore Form 8839 line 14 plus /adoptionCarryforwardIn (every prior lot), not line 16, and a lot that cannot be claimed this year still carries to 2026 until the five-year window ends it (IRC 23(c)(1)-(2); TAX-INTERPRETATIONS CR-12). On every other return line 16 is line 14 plus /adoptionCarryforwardIn, so nothing else moves. A separate return that cannot use any of its carryforward (the credit is not active) spends nothing, so it carries every lot except the 2020 lot. THE $0 ARM. The last case is taken whenever /adoptionCreditIsActive is false and the return is not such a separate return with a carryforward: every return with no Form 8839 input at all.

Fact.Name: Refusal: the 2020 adoption credit carryforward answered is larger than Form 8839 line 15
Fact.Description:
The filer answered a 2020-vintage carryforward larger than the whole prior-year carryforward they entered on Form 8839 line 15. The 2020 lot is a PART of line 15 — the worksheet's line 7 adds lines 2 through 6 to the current-year amount and line 15 is those prior-year lots together — so the two answers contradict each other and the graph cannot tell which is wrong. It matters in dollars: the worksheet subtracts the surviving 2020 lot at line 22, so an overstated vintage understates the carryforward going to 2026.
AN INPUT CONTRADICTION, not a scope gap. Nothing is unbuilt behind it; either answer alone computes. It clears the moment the filer corrects one of the two figures, which is why it carries no successor obligation beyond the two questions already being asked.
COMPLETE-FALSE, never Incomplete, on every return that does not answer the 2020 question: the leading conjunct is IsComplete over that writable, so an unanswered vintage resolves this false without evaluating the comparison.

Fact.Name: Adoption of this child became final in 2025 or earlier (Form 8839 Part I line 1 column (g))
Fact.Description: SCREEN: "Did the adoption of this child become final in 2025 or earlier?" — the column (g) box in this child's Part I row. HELP: this records only the FINALITY of the adoption; it is distinct from ../writableHasSpecialNeeds, which asserts the special-needs determination that drives the full per-child amount on line 5. ASKED WHEN: once per item in /form8839Children, and it MUST be asked whenever ../writableChildIsForeignChild is answered Yes, because for a foreign child it is the question that decides the credit and the exclusion. VALIDATION: Yes/No. UNANSWERED (three-state): the printed box stays unchecked — the correct state for an adoption still pending at the end of 2025 — and ../childAdoptionFinalIn2025OrEarlier resolves false. CONSUMER AND MONEY CONSEQUENCE: on a foreign child, unanswered or unchecked is what makes ../childForeignAndNotFinal true, zeroing ../line2 (the credit) and ../line19 (the exclusion) for this child. Silence deliberately does NOT grant the benefit here: section 23(e)(1) requires finality before either is available, and an unanswered box cannot prove it. On a domestic child no computation reads this box.

Fact.Name: Eligible child born before 2008 and disabled (Form 8839 Part I line 1 column (c))
Fact.Description: SCREEN: "Was this child born before 2008 AND physically or mentally unable to care for themselves?" — the column (c) box in this child's Part I row, which the printed form states as ONE compound condition, so it takes one Yes/No answer. HELP: a disabled individual, one who is physically or mentally unable to care for themselves, is an eligible child regardless of their age at the time of adoption (i8839 Column (c)); that is why an adult adoptee can still support a credit. ASKED WHEN: once per item in /form8839Children, on the same Part I screen as the year of birth — and it is the question that decides the credit for any child whose ../writableChildYearOfBirth is 2006 or earlier. VALIDATION: Yes/No. UNANSWERED (three-state): the printed box stays unchecked and ../childBornBefore2008AndDisabled resolves false, the ordinary case for a child under 18. CONSUMER AND MONEY CONSEQUENCE: ../childMeetsEligibleChildDefinition reads it as the SOLE eligibility path for a child who fails ../childAgeEligible; unchecked on such a child sends ../line2 and the whole Part II credit chain for that child to $0. Checked, it restores the full chain no matter how old the child is.

Fact.Name: Eligible child first name (Form 8839 Part I line 1 column (a))

Fact.Name: Eligible child is a foreign child (Form 8839 Part I line 1 column (e))
Fact.Description: SCREEN: "Was this child a foreign child — not a citizen or resident of the United States or its territories when the adoption effort began?" — the column (e) box in this child's Part I row. HELP: the form's Part I caution routes a foreign child through the Special Rules before either Part II or Part III, and i8839 Column (e) requires the column (g) finality box to be answered whenever this box is checked. ASKED WHEN: once per item in /form8839Children, on the Part I screen; a Yes here MUST be followed on the same screen by column (g) (../writableChildAdoptionFinalIn2025OrEarlier). VALIDATION: Yes/No. UNANSWERED (three-state): the printed box stays unchecked and ../childIsForeignChild resolves false, so a silent column never bars a domestic adoption. CONSUMER AND MONEY CONSEQUENCE: with column (g) unchecked or unanswered, a Yes here makes ../childForeignAndNotFinal true, which bars BOTH halves of the form for this child — ../line2 goes to $0 (no credit) and ../line19 goes to $0 (no exclusion, so this child's employer-provided benefits stay fully taxable and reach Form 1040 line 1f in full). A Yes with column (g) checked leaves both chains untouched.

Fact.Name: Eligible child last name (Form 8839 Part I line 1 column (a))
Fact.Description: The eligible child's LAST name as printed in this child's Part I row, column (a), which the form splits into a First box and a Last box. Faithful record only; no computation reads it. OPTIONAL (three-state): unanswered leaves the printed box blank.

Fact.Name: Eligible child identifying number (Form 8839 Part I line 1 column (f))
